The Australian smelt (Retropinna semoni) is a small freshwater fish that rarely exceeds an ultimate total length of 10 cm [Li = 10 cm], a diminutive size typical of many osmeriform species inhabiting lowland rivers and streams in southeastern Australia. Field surveys across the Murray-Darling Basin have consistently documented that individuals approaching this maximum length are typically several years old, reflecting the relatively slow growth trajectory of this species in temperate environments. The relationship between length and mass in this species follows a power-law function, with the ultimate wet weight of the largest recorded adults reaching approximately 5.12 grams [Wwi = approximately 5.12 grams]. This modest body mass is consistent with the species' position as a mid-level forage fish in its native food webs, where it serves as a critical prey item for larger piscivorous fishes, waterbirds, and platypus. Growth rates vary considerably across its latitudinal range, with populations in cooler, upland streams tending to attain smaller adult sizes compared to those in warmer lowland habitats, likely due to differences in growing season duration and food availability.

Sexual maturation in Australian smelt is closely tied to body size rather than age, with individuals typically reaching total length at puberty of 4.99 cm [Lp = 4.99 cm], a threshold that corresponds to approximately one year of growth under typical thermal regimes. At this developmental milestone, the body composition shifts markedly as resources begin to be directed toward gonadal development. The corresponding wet weight at puberty has been estimated at 0.59 grams [Wwp = 0.59 grams], representing a more than thousand-fold increase from the mass at the earliest life stages. Studies examining the size structure of spawning aggregations have confirmed that very few individuals below this length threshold exhibit active gametogenesis, supporting the interpretation that this length represents a genuine maturation benchmark. Comparisons with related retropinnid species suggest that the Australian smelt matures at a relatively small size, an adaptation that may facilitate rapid population turnover in unpredictable hydrological environments where early reproduction carries a selective advantage.

Egg diameter measurements from gravid females indicate that the wet weight at birth is approximately 0.000449 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.000449 grams], a value derived from the average diameter of the demersal, adhesive eggs which measure about 0.95 mm across. These small, yolk-laden eggs are deposited during broadcast spawning events onto submerged vegetation and gravel substrates, where they undergo embryonic development over a period of roughly 7 to 10 days depending on ambient temperature. The newly hatched yolk-sac larvae are transparent and measure only a few millimeters in total length, relying entirely on endogenous yolk reserves during their first several days of life. This minute neonatal mass places Australian smelt at the lower end of the range for freshwater teleost species, reflecting a life-history strategy that prioritizes high fecundity over per-offspring investment. The energetic cost of producing such small propagules is relatively low per individual, allowing females to partition their reproductive investment across many thousands of eggs each season.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a stable water temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the maximum reproductive rate of Australian smelt has been estimated at approximately 1050 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 1050 eggs per year]. This sustained reproductive output, which translates to roughly 2.9 eggs per day, is achieved through repeated spawning events in quick succession by gravid females. The high annual fecundity is facilitated by the species' relatively small egg size and rapid oocyte development cycle, which allows females to mature successive cohorts of eggs within a single season. Field validation studies conducted in the Murray River have confirmed that individual females can spawn multiple times across the protracted spring-summer breeding period, though actual realized fecundity in the wild is often lower than the laboratory maximum due to food limitation and variable thermal conditions. The capacity for high reproductive output is a key life-history trait that enables Australian smelt to recover quickly from population crashes following drought or flood events.

The maximum lifespan recorded for Australian smelt under natural conditions is approximately 3 years [am = approximately 3 years], when evaluated at a mean water temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], though some individuals in cooler, stable upland populations may persist for up to four years. This relatively short longevity is typical of small-bodied, iteroparous freshwater fishes that exhibit rapid maturation and high reproductive effort. The species shows pronounced senescence in its third year, with older individuals displaying reduced condition factors, diminished gonadal investment, and increased susceptibility to parasitic infections. Life-table analyses indicate that mortality rates increase sharply after the second spawning season, with very few fish surviving to a third reproductive bout. This compressed lifespan, coupled with early maturation and high fecundity, positions Australian smelt as an opportunistic strategist well suited to the hydrologically variable environments of the Murray-Darling Basin, where the ability to colonize newly inundated habitats quickly is critical for population persistence.
